mcqs.question: Let P and Q be two statements. Which of the following correctly describes the truth value of the compound statement "P \u2228 Q" (P or Q)?

options.A: It is true only when both P and Q are true.
options.B: It is false only when both P and Q are false.
options.C: It is true only when exactly one of P or Q is true.
options.D: It is false when at least one of P or Q is true.

mcqs.answer: It is false only when both P and Q are false.
mcqs.explanation: For a disjunction (P \u2228 Q) the only case when it is false is when both components are false; in all other cases (one true or both true) the disjunction is true. Hence option B is correct, while the other options misstate the truth condition.

mcqs.question: Consider the implication "If it rains, then the ground gets wet" represented as P \u2192 Q. Which of the following rows gives a correct truth‑value pair for P, Q and the implication P \u2192 Q?

options.A: P is true, Q is true, and P \u2192 Q is false.
options.B: P is true, Q is false, and P \u2192 Q is false.
options.C: P is false, Q is true, and P \u2192 Q is false.
options.D: P is false, Q is false, and P \u2192 Q is true.

mcqs.answer: P is true, Q is false, and P \u2192 Q is false.
mcqs.explanation: An implication P \u2192 Q is false only when the antecedent P is true and the consequent Q is false. All other combinations make the implication true. Therefore option B correctly captures the only false case; the other options either give wrong truth values for the implication or mis‑represent the condition.

mcqs.question: Which statement correctly compares the biconditional "P \u2194 Q" with the expression "(P \u2227 Q) \u2228 (\u00acP \u2227 \u00acQ)"?

options.A: They are not equivalent; the biconditional is true only when both P and Q are true.
options.B: They are equivalent because both are true exactly when P and Q have the same truth value.
options.C: The biconditional is true only when P and Q are both false, whereas the expression is true only when both are true.
options.D: The biconditional is true when at least one of P or Q is true, while the expression is true only when both are false.

mcqs.answer: They are equivalent because both are true exactly when P and Q have the same truth value.
mcqs.explanation: A biconditional P \u2194 Q is true when P and Q are both true or both false. The expression (P \u2227 Q) \u2228 (\u00acP \u2227 \u00acQ) captures the same two cases, making the two statements logically equivalent. Options A, C, and D misstate the truth conditions.

mcqs.question: Given the compound statement \((P \u2228 Q) \u2192 (P \u2227 R)\), what is its truth value when P is false, Q is true and R is false?

options.D: Depends on the truth value of R

mcqs.explanation: First evaluate the antecedent: P \u2228 Q = false \u2228 true = true. The consequent: P \u2227 R = false \u2227 false = false. An implication true \u2192 false is false. Hence the whole statement is false, making option B correct. The other options ignore the implication rule.

mcqs.question: Which of the following correctly defines the logical conjunction "P \u2227 Q"?

options.A: It is true only when both P and Q are true.
options.B: It is true when at least one of P or Q is true.
options.C: It is false only when both P and Q are false.
options.D: It is true when exactly one of P or Q is true.

mcqs.answer: It is true only when both P and Q are true.
mcqs.explanation: Conjunction (P \u2227 Q) requires both component statements to be true for the whole to be true; any false component makes the conjunction false. Option A states this precisely, while the other options describe disjunction or other incorrect conditions.

mcqs.question: The logical disjunction "P \u2228 Q" is true in which of the following situations?

options.A: Only when both P and Q are true.
options.B: When at least one of P or Q is true.
options.C: Only when exactly one of P or Q is true.
options.D: When both P and Q are false.

mcqs.answer: When at least one of P or Q is true.
mcqs.explanation: A disjunction is false only when both components are false; in every other case (one true or both true) it is true. Therefore option B correctly captures the condition. Options A and C are too restrictive, and D describes the false case.

mcqs.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes the implication "P \u2192 Q" from its converse "Q \u2192 P"?

options.A: P \u2192 Q is true when P is false or Q is true; the converse swaps the roles of P and Q.
options.B: P \u2192 Q is true only when both P and Q are true; the converse is always false.
options.C: P \u2192 Q is false only when P is true and Q is false; the converse has the same truth condition.
options.D: There is no difference; implication and its converse are logically identical.

mcqs.answer: P \u2192 Q is true when P is false or Q is true; the converse swaps the roles of P and Q.
mcqs.explanation: An implication P \u2192 Q is false only in the case P true and Q false; otherwise it is true. The converse Q \u2192 P simply interchanges antecedent and consequent, so its truth conditions are based on Q and P respectively. Option A states this accurately. Option B misstates the condition, C incorrectly claims both have identical truth tables, and D ignores the difference.

mcqs.question: Which of the following sentences correctly uses a biconditional ("if and only if") relationship?

options.A: If a number is even, then its square is even.
options.B: If a number's square is even, then the number is even.
options.C: A number is even if and only if its square is even.

mcqs.answer: A number is even if and only if its square is even.
mcqs.explanation: The phrase "if and only if" denotes a biconditional, meaning both directions hold: a number being even implies its square is even, and conversely, an even square implies the number is even. Option C captures this two‑way relationship. Options A and B each state only one direction, not a biconditional, and D is therefore incorrect.
